newsitem.title: HUNGARY: POLICE BLAMES PRESS FOR HUNGARY BOMB BLASTS.
newsitem.headline: POLICE BLAMES PRESS FOR HUNGARY BOMB BLASTS.

text.p: The Hungarian police on Wednesday partly blamed press reports for a series of bomb blasts which have killed one and injured at least four in the last ten days.
Press reports generated fear of terrorist acts among the population and encouraged potential bombers, police spokesman Andras Ruzsa said.
"The press gives blanket coverage of these explosions," Ruzsa told Reuters. "Perhaps it shouldn't...Young men, people who are inclined to do such things read it and they may happen to try it."
A pipe bomb, which went off in a parking lot damaging several cars on Tuesday night in Veszprem, Western Hungary, was the fourth explosion since October 5.
The daily Magyar Hirlap said on Tuesday that the police investigated 28 blasts in the past seven years and as many as 13 hand grenades and other explosive devices blew up this year.
Ruzsa denied that the blasts have become more frequent but did not exclude the possibility that the recent spate could continue.
On Saturday night a Slovak youth was killed by a blast in Budapest and the Hungarian and the Slovak police are trying to extablish whnmether it was suicide or not.

One week ago another bomb, planted in a dustbin near Europe's largest synagogue, exploded in Budapest, raising concerns in the Jewish community as it was the second blast in the vicinity of the synagogue since August 25.
The police on Tuesday detained a 17-year-old man who confessed to planting a bomb under a seat in a bus earlier this month, Ruzsa said.
The blast injured four people and it could have also killed but for the doors of the bus being open at the moment of the explosion, the police told a news conference on Tuesday.
The police said they believed the man could have exploded further bombs to underline his demands for money to businessmen he threatened with blowing up.

Ruzsa said that suicide or revenge, often between criminal gangs, were the most typical motivation of bomb blasts in Hungary in the past few years, adding the police did not have evidence that terrorist groups worked in the country.
He added that the police also did not have any evidence of political or religious reasons for blasts and suppositions of that kind belonged to the realm of press speculation.
